# Comedy — Part 2

Continues category `comedy`. Part 1 is in `cat-comedy.md`.

**Part 2 of 2.** 39 cards across character comedy, the comic scene, wordplay and its limits, comic structure at length, tone control, improv principles that transfer to writing, audience and offence, and four more named failures.

Part 1 took comedy apart at the level of the joke. This file works at the level of the person telling it, the scene it sits in, the season it has to survive, and the room it is aimed at.

## Section 1 — Character Comedy

### Name the Engine Before the Joke

**Also called:** the comedy selector, engine before joke, what is generating this
**What it is:** The card at the head of the `comedy.` shelf. It does not describe a comic style. It asks the three questions the shelf's own pair graph asks over and over — **how long this has to keep producing, who is making the joke and whether they know it is one, and what the laugh spends** — and hands back a named shortlist for each answer. The axes were not invented: they were read off the fifty-seven `Yields to:` conditions the cards carry and cross-checked against every `Avoid when:` line on the shelf, and the conditions that repeated became the questions. Every card cited here is cited by id.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card never reaches the page. It exists so that the joke that does reach the page was chosen against the runtime, the speaker and the bill, rather than written because it arrived.
**Used for and where it works best:** Answer the three questions **in order and out loud, in one sentence each, before you write a line of comedy**. Question one alone cuts the shelf by roughly two-thirds, because a machine that must still be generating at episode forty and a gag that is spent in one exchange share almost nothing. Questions two and three leave a shortlist of three to six. If you cannot answer question one — *how long must this keep producing* — you do not yet have a comic problem, you have a tone note. Where two answers fight for one scene, that is two comic decisions and one of them is `comedy.when_to_stop`.
**Best in:** formats: all | genres: all
**Avoid when:** **The scene is already funny and has stopped working.** Then the route in is the failure, not this map: `comedy.joke_that_stops_story`, `comedy.only_funny_character`, `comedy.audience_gets_there_first`, `comedy.explained_joke`, `comedy.sympathy_cost_joke`, `comedy.reference_not_joke`, `comedy.quirk_as_character` and `comedy.requires_agreement` each name their own repair in their own line, and none of them appears below, because a selector that listed a failure would be offering to fail. Also avoid it when you are writing **the line rather than the machine** — whose mouth a joke comes out of is settled on the `dial.` shelf, and this one settles only what shape the joke is. And **distrust axis two whenever your honest answer is its third value**: thirty of the sixty-two cards live there, so on a piece where the writer is making all the jokes over the characters' heads this map has two questions left and is doing a third less work than it looks like it is doing.
**Example:**
> A ten-minute diaspora short, one funeral, two brothers.
>
> One: the whole piece, used up by the end — not a beat, not a season.
> Two: the characters, sincerely — neither of them is doing a bit.
> Three: the piece's own footing — it has to still be a funeral at the end.
>
> The intersection is four cards wide: `comedy.generative_pairing`, `comedy.tragedy_in_comedy`, `comedy.turn_serious_and_back`, `comedy.when_to_stop`. Nothing about jokes was decided, and the joke shape is now a small question instead of a blank page.

---

**The axes**

**Axis 1 — How long does this have to keep producing?**
Asked first, because it is the condition the shelf repeats most and the one that eliminates fastest. Eighteen of the `Yields to:` lines turn on runtime or renewal, and they are stated as facts rather than tastes: *"the story asks this character to genuinely change"* (`comedy.comic_character_engine`), *"a feature, and you have built a series premise by accident"* (`comedy.premise_shelf_life`), *"the audience will watch four episodes in a row"* (`comedy.reset_cost`), *"the structure requires them apart for a whole act"* (`comedy.generative_pairing`), *"the gag has no variation available"* (`comedy.running_gag`), *"the audience has to remember two things at once"* (`comedy.callback_payoff`), *"the piece is under thirty seconds"* (`comedy.heighten_and_explore`), *"you have already used it in the last two minutes"* (`comedy.rule_of_three`).

**Axis 2 — Who is making the joke, and do they know it is one?**
Fifteen conditions turn on this, and the shelf states it as a reciprocal pair rather than a preference: `comedy.literal_answer` yields on *"the misread is a weapon, not innocence"* and `comedy.technically_correct` yields straight back on *"the misread is innocent, not a weapon"*. The same fork runs through *"your character is knowingly performing the mismatch"* (`comedy.wrong_place`), *"the comic character is already self-aware"* (`comedy.straight_man`), *"the speaker must not be joking"* and *"the whole piece is already written in a heightened register"* (`comedy.register_collision`, from both sides), and *"the world is meant to be uniformly absurd"* (`comedy.first_unusual_thing`).

**Axis 3 — What does the laugh spend?**
Fourteen conditions are about the bill, not the laugh: *"you have no plan for what the laugh costs"* (`comedy.setup_punchline`), *"farce burns sympathy as fuel"* (`comedy.farce_engine`), *"the character has no dignity left to lose"* (`comedy.cringe`), *"the audience is currently inside the event"* (`comedy.dark_comedy`), *"the audience is meant to be on the questioner's side"* (`comedy.technically_correct`), *"this character must carry the emotional climax"* (`comedy.wrong_reaction`), *"the delusion is harming someone in the room and the piece has not decided how it feels about that"* (`comedy.maintained_delusion`), *"you will not pay it off"* (`comedy.tragedy_in_comedy`), *"the next scene opens on grief or violence"* (`comedy.exit_joke`). It is asked last because it is the only axis that reaches the tone block at all, and because most of the shelf answers it the same way.

**The default, and the one against it**

**The default is `comedy.deliberate_stop`, and it is measured rather than asserted.** Three cards send a reader to it and each fires on a different condition: `comedy.wrong_reaction` (*"this character must carry the emotional climax"*), `comedy.exit_joke` (*"the next scene opens on grief or violence"*) and `comedy.turn_serious_and_back` (*"the turn is inside one scene, not across the piece"*). One is a character-construction card, one is a scene-shape card, one is a tone card. Nothing else on this shelf is reached from three unlike places — the nearest rivals take two — and the distinction matters, because `comedy.translation_resistance` is reached three times as well and all three edges say the same thing: the work is crossing a language. **That is a door out of the shelf, not a fallback.** Count the conditions and not the edges, and this shelf's fallback is the decision to stop.

**And read what that means rather than only recording it.** The shelf, asked what to do when a comic choice will not hold, most often answers: *take the machine out of gear, inside the scene, on purpose, and let the truth through the door they were holding open for a joke.* A lighting shelf falls back to a light. This one falls back to silence — which is the shelf telling you, in its own hand, that comedy's commonest repair is not another joke.

**A near-miss worth recording, because its evidence is contested.** `comedy.game_of_the_scene` is reached twice on two unlike conditions and would be second. One of those two edges comes from `comedy.timing_on_the_page`, which is one of the cards a blind re-read judged to carry a pair field that is not a pair at all. **On the conservative reading its routing is contested and `comedy.game_of_the_scene` has one uncontested inbound edge; on the permissive reading it has two and is the runner-up.** No side is picked here. The same caution attaches to `comedy.joke_shelf_life`, reached from `comedy.dark_comedy` and from a named failure, and to `comedy.premise_shelf_life`, which reaches `comedy.season_engine` and is reached by nothing.

**The one against it is `comedy.deliberate_cliche`.** Nothing routes to it, it routes to nothing, and it inverts the premise every other card on this shelf shares. Everything else here makes comedy by **constructing** something — a game, a lie, a pattern, a spiral, a collision. This one makes comedy by constructing nothing: the character speaks entirely in dead phrases and the emptiness is the content, so the writing has to be flat on purpose at exactly the moment a real sentence is owed. Its own `Avoid when:` names the cost with unusual precision — the technique and the defect are typographically identical and the only difference is placement — which is also why nothing can route to it: a pointer would be pointing at a line indistinguishable from bad writing. Its near cousin against the grain is `comedy.status_engine`, which carries no alternative at all and whose own line reads *never avoid it, but never narrate it* — the shelf's one claim that a scene can be funny with no joke anywhere in it.

**The unasked**

**Twenty-nine of the sixty-two reachable cards are the target of no `Yields to:` field anywhere on this shelf.** They can be chosen; nothing ever sends you to them. By id:

`comedy.setup_punchline` · `comedy.rule_of_three` · `comedy.misdirection` · `comedy.non_sequitur` · `comedy.observational_truth` · `comedy.timing_on_the_page` · `comedy.status_engine` · `comedy.wrong_reaction` · `comedy.dark_comedy` · `comedy.physical_on_page` · `comedy.kids_comedy` · `comedy.comic_flaw` · `comedy.airtight_wrong_logic` · `comedy.maintained_delusion` · `comedy.useless_expertise` · `comedy.escalating_obligation` · `comedy.wrong_place` · `comedy.comic_entrance` · `comedy.pun_legitimacy` · `comedy.malapropism` · `comedy.deliberate_cliche` · `comedy.premise_shelf_life` · `comedy.reset_cost` · `comedy.last_joke_before_death` · `comedy.when_to_stop` · `comedy.heighten_and_explore` · `comedy.first_unusual_thing` · `comedy.punch_direction` · `comedy.cross_cultural_comedy`

**And the shape of that list is the finding, not its length.** Two blocks fall inside it whole.

**The first is the joke unit.** `comedy.setup_punchline`, `comedy.rule_of_three`, `comedy.misdirection`, `comedy.non_sequitur`, `comedy.observational_truth` and `comedy.timing_on_the_page` all yield outward and nothing yields inward. The pair graph is a graph of **machines**: a reader comparing two comic approaches is comparing two engines, and nobody on this shelf ever wrote *not this joke — that joke*. The unit cards point up into the engines and the engines never point back down. That is why axis one is asked first, and why its first value — the beat — is the value this map can tell you least about.

**The second is the comic person, and it is the more serious gap.** `comedy.comic_flaw`, `comedy.maintained_delusion`, `comedy.status_engine`, `comedy.wrong_reaction`, `comedy.useless_expertise` and `comedy.airtight_wrong_logic` are the six cards that build a character who will still be funny in hour two. Every one is unasked, and three of them carry no `Yields to:` at all. The shelf can route you to a structure, a mode, a tone and a stopping point, and it has **no route whatever into building the person**. The nearest thing that exists, `comedy.comic_character_engine`, is reached from `comedy.comic_ending` — that is, from the far end of the piece, by a reader already worrying about the finale — and otherwise only from a named failure. **The new card this shelf wants is the one that asks which kind of comic person this is before asking what they say**, and it does not exist: the six cards that would answer it sit in a block nothing on the shelf points at.

A third, smaller shape: **every wordplay card is unasked** — `comedy.pun_legitimacy`, `comedy.malapropism`, `comedy.deliberate_cliche`. Words are where readers agree comedy is weakest, and where the shelf's own pointers have nothing at all to say.

`comedy.engine_before_the_joke`

### The Comic Flaw

**Also called:** the funny weakness, the productive defect, the engine fault
**What it is:** A single character weakness chosen because it reliably produces bad decisions, not because it is psychologically realistic. The flaw is not a wound waiting to be healed; it is a machine part.
**Effect on the audience:** Anticipation. Once they have the flaw, they read every new situation twice — once as it is, and once as the way this person is about to mishandle it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any lead who has to be funny across more than one scene. The craft rule is a test: drop the character into three unrelated situations — a funeral, a job interview, a supermarket queue — and check that the flaw produces a *different* bad decision in each. A flaw that only functions in one setting is a joke, not an engine. Keep it adjacent to something the character is genuinely good at (`char.incompetence_zone`), so they are not merely useless.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Feature Film, Animated Series, Novel | genres: Comedy, Satire, Workplace, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** The story wants us to admire this person at the end without paying for it. A flaw that costs nothing is a quirk — see `comedy.quirk_as_character`.
**Example:**
> Three situations, one flaw: he cannot bear to be the least informed person in a room.
>
> At the funeral: "I actually knew him before most of you. Well — of him."
> At the interview: "I'm familiar with the software, yes. Which one is it again, so I know which of the two I'm thinking of."
> In the supermarket queue: "That's not the quick lane. I'd not normally say anything."

`comedy.comic_flaw`

---

### Airtight Logic, Wrong Premise

**Also called:** the consistent madman, valid but unsound, the reasonable lunatic
**What it is:** A character reasons perfectly from a starting assumption that is insane, and never breaks the chain. Every step is defensible. Only the first one is wrong, and nobody thinks to go back and check it.
**Effect on the audience:** The specific helplessness of being unable to refute something obviously false. That is a much bigger laugh than nonsense, because nonsense can be dismissed and this cannot.
**Used for and where it works best:** Bureaucrats, zealots, conspiracists, children, lawyers, machines. The craft rule: write the false premise as one sentence at the top of the page and never let the character say it out loud. They only ever state conclusions. The moment they articulate the premise, the audience can argue with it and the comedy turns into a debate. Give them a `comedy.straight_man` who attacks the conclusions and never once attacks the premise.
**Best in:** formats: Sketch, Half-Hour Comedy, Stage Play, Animated Series, Novel | genres: Comedy, Satire, Farce, Workplace
**Avoid when:** The audience is later asked to take this character's side on a plot question. Airtight-and-wrong is entertaining and completely untrustworthy; you cannot borrow credibility back from it.
**Example:**
> "You can't charge me for a second bag. I checked one."
> "You checked two, sir."
> "I checked one twice. Your system logged it twice. That's your system's problem, not my bag's."
> "Both bags are here."
> "Then one of them isn't mine, and I'd like to know what you've put in it."

**Yields to:** `comedy.technically_correct` — The audience must still trust this character later.  
`comedy.airtight_wrong_logic`

---

### The Maintained Delusion

**Also called:** the fantasy self, the unrevised self-image, the upkeep
**What it is:** The extension of `comedy.comic_character_engine` into behaviour. Where that card names the lie a comic character tells about themselves, this one is about the daily labour of keeping the lie standing — because the comedy is in the maintenance, not the belief.
**Effect on the audience:** Affection laced with alarm. The cost is what converts a delusion from a gag into a person; we laugh at the work and we recognise the work.
**Used for and where it works best:** Leads in long-running comedy, and any character the audience has to like for hours. The craft rule: every scene shows exactly one act of maintenance the character believes nobody noticed — a receipt palmed, a name dropped, a story quietly re-edited. Second rule: the delusion must never be punctured from outside. Only the character can put it down, once, very late, which is precisely why they mostly do not (`char.cannot_change`).
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Novel, Feature Film, Stage Play | genres: Comedy, Satire, Family Drama, Workplace
**Avoid when:** The delusion is harming someone in the room and the piece has not decided how it feels about that. An unexamined delusion with a victim reads as the writer siding with the deluded.
**Example:**
> "We don't advertise. Word of mouth."
> "You've got a sign in the window."
> "That's not advertising. That's the window telling people what the shop is."
> "It says FIFTY PERCENT OFF."
> "That's the window being honest. If anything it's the opposite of advertising."

`comedy.maintained_delusion`

---

### The Specialist in Something Useless

**Also called:** the expert nobody needs, misapplied mastery, the wrong genius
**What it is:** A character with deep, genuine, verifiable expertise in a domain the story has no use for, who applies it anyway, at length, to everything.
**Effect on the audience:** Two pleasures at once — real competence, which audiences always enjoy, and its total irrelevance, which is the joke.
**Used for and where it works best:** Ensembles that need a generator which does not wear out, since the domain is inexhaustible. The craft rule: the expertise must be real and researched, because invented expertise produces no detail and detail is where the jokes are (`char.trade_vocabulary`). Second rule: let the useless skill work exactly once, very late, in a way that solves something small. The audience has been investing for an hour and that is the repayment.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Feature Film, Animated Series, Podcast | genres: Comedy, Workplace, Crime, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** The domain is one your audience knows better than you do. Then every detail is a correction, and a corrected expert is not funny, only wrong.
**Example:**
> "The kidnappers will call between six and seven."
> "Landline or mobile?"
> "Does it matter?"
> "It's a 1987 Trimphone. If it's the landline I can tell you which exchange they're in from the ring. If it's the mobile I can tell you nothing, and I'll be honest with you, I'd rather it was the landline."

**Yields to:** `comedy.register_collision` — The audience knows the domain better than you do.  
`comedy.useless_expertise`

---

### The Pairing That Generates Jokes Structurally

**Also called:** the comic duo, the built-in argument, the two-person engine
**What it is:** Two characters whose defining beliefs are incompatible in a way that produces conflict about literally anything. The pairing is the machine; the individual lines are only its output.
**Effect on the audience:** They look forward to the combination before either character has spoken. That anticipation is worth more than any single joke in the scene.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any comedy that must keep producing for a season or a franchise. The craft rule: build the pair so they disagree about a *method*, not a *goal*. Two people who want different things simply leave the room. Two people who want the same thing by opposite methods are stuck together, which is where comedy lives. Test it by putting them in a scene with no plot at all — waiting for a bus — and seeing whether a scene happens (`scene.two_hander`, `comedy.status_engine`). If nothing happens, the pairing is decorative.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Feature Film, Animated Series, Stage Play, Podcast | genres: Comedy, Farce, Crime, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** The structure requires them apart for a whole act. A structurally generative pair is inert when separated, and the episode that splits them is always the weak one — write it deliberately or not at all.
**Example:**
> Both want the funeral to go well.
>
> "I've made a list of who speaks."
> "People will speak when they're moved to speak."
> "Then put that on the list and I'll give it a time."
> "You can't time being moved."
> "I've given it eleven minutes. That's generous, Nabil. That's more than Mum got at Dad's."

**Yields to:** `comedy.ab_collision` — where the structure requires them apart for a whole act. A structurally generative pair is inert when separated, and the episode that splits them is always the weak one.  
`comedy.generative_pairing`
